Gastroenterology · published research

Hepatic encephalopathy

Summary of the Evidence

Two related rat publications from one Spanish research group examined transcranial PBM in models of minimal or overt hepatic encephalopathy. Both reported improved stimulus-response memory after seven daily treatments. They are separate experiments from the same laboratory rather than independent replications, and neither tested liver function or patient outcomes (Arias et al. 2016; Méndez et al. 2021).

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical trial has tested PBM for hepatic encephalopathy in people. The animal outcomes concern memory-task performance and regional brain metabolism. They do not establish improved liver function, fewer encephalopathy episodes, or better daily functioning in patients.

Animal evidence

The 2016 experiment included 21 rats assigned to sham, portal-hypertension, or portal-hypertension plus PBM groups. Seven daily 670-nm LED exposures at 9 J/cm² improved acquisition of a stimulus-response task compared with untreated portal-hypertension animals. Cytochrome-c-oxidase activity differed across brain regions, while network patterns in treated animals were more similar to sham controls (Arias et al. 2016).

The 2021 experiment used five groups totaling 34 rats and compared PBM with intracranial methylene blue. Both treatments improved the experimental memory deficit. PBM produced lower cytochrome-c-oxidase activity than methylene blue in several analysed regions, showing that behavioral improvement did not correspond to a uniform increase in this metabolic marker (Méndez et al. 2021).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Both experiments used transcranial 670 ± 10 nm red LED light at 9 J/cm² once daily for seven days. Neither compared wavelengths, doses, or schedules. Rat skull transmission and the portal-hypertension or hepatic-encephalopathy models do not establish how much light would reach relevant human brain regions or whether cognitive findings would translate to clinical episodes.

Interpretation

The two experiments provide a consistent behavioral signal within related rat models, while the metabolic findings are region-specific and depend on the comparator. Because both publications come from one group and no human study was identified, certainty remains very low and the results do not establish PBM as a treatment for hepatic encephalopathy.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)Very low for short-term memory performance in rat models of minimal hepatic encephalopathy

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Two rat experiments from one Spanish research group reported better stimulus-response memory after transcranial 670-nm PBM. Both used a seven-day, 9-J/cm² schedule, and the later experiment found different regional cytochrome-c-oxidase responses with PBM and methylene blue. No patient study or independent laboratory replication was identified, so certainty remains very low.
